title: 1.1 · Everyone measures one block
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.1 · Everyone measures one block

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can describe the spread in a set of measurements and sketch what I measured with the proportions right.MEASURE 40 · DRAW 40 · HAND IT OVER 30☐ Tapes, one each ☐ Blank paper ☐ Fieldhouse access ☐ Board
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15Go to the fieldhouse. No preamble. Everyone puts a tape on the same block in the wall and writes down its length. Every reading goes on the board when you get back — or on a clipboard right there.RememberPrior knowledge · d=0.41
15–40

One block, twenty numbers. Why don't we agree? Rough face, where you hook, reading at an angle, whether you included the mortar. Test the ones you can.

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “You got 15 1/2 and he got 15 3/4. One of you is wrong — or neither is. Which?” · Revoice.

AnalyzeClassroom discussion · d=0.82
40–80

Freehand sketch of the block. No straightedge. Proportions first, then your measurements on it.

ELL/SWD: sketch with no numbers at all first, then add them. Two passes, not one.

ApplyCooperative learning · d=0.55
80–110Trade sketches. Could the other person order that block from your drawing? Count the questions they have to ask — that number is the quality of your drawing.EvaluatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Nobody will get 16. The block is called 16 and measures about 15 5/8. Do not resolve that today — it is the hook for the whole unit and it should sit unresolved for a week.

Question count on the handover is the number to record. It gets compared in 1.3.

MATERIALS & PREP

One tape per student. Confirm fieldhouse access and pick the wall in advance.

Blank unlined paper. Graph paper makes them draw squares instead of looking.

Have a clipboard so readings get recorded at the wall, not from memory.

TEACHER NOTES

Someone will say “it's supposed to be 16.” Write that on the board and leave it there for two weeks.

Do not correct technique in the first fifteen minutes. The spread has to happen honestly.

title: 1.2 · Reading to 1/16
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.2 · Reading to 1/16

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can read a tape or rule to 1/16 and write it correctly.15 + 25 + 15☐ Packets ☐ Rules ☐ Tapes
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15

Tallest mark is the inch. Halve down: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16. Teach it as counting marks and naming what you counted — not as fractions.

ELL/SWD: trace the tick heights with a finger before naming anything.

UnderstandWorked examples · d=0.57
15–40Nine readings in the packet. Whole number and fraction. Then reading rounds — you put one on the board, they write, reveal, score. Twenty in ten minutes.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
40–55Back to the block. Is it 15 1/2, 15 5/8 or 15 3/4? Half the disagreement yesterday was people who could not read to a sixteenth.AnalyzeSpaced retrieval · d=0.65
FORMATIVE CHECKS

The reading rounds give you twenty data points per student in ten minutes. Use them.

Watch for students who point at the right mark and then write 3 1/3.

MATERIALS & PREP

Print the rule graphic full size. A shrunk one is useless.

Prepare fifteen reading calls in advance so the rounds move fast. No calculators.

TEACHER NOTESFractions are the math spine of this unit and this is where they get established.

title: 1.3 · The hook, and where the numbers go
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.3 · The hook, and where the numbers go

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can explain why the hook slides, check whether mine is true, and dimension a drawing to convention.MEASURE 35 · DRAW 45 · HAND IT OVER 30☐ Tapes ☐ Calipers ☐ Known block ☐ 1.1 sketches
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–10“Pull the hook on your tape.” Wait. Let them find it.RememberPrior knowledge · d=0.41
10–35

How far does it slide? Measure it. Now measure the hook's thickness. Same number. Then measure a door opening two ways — hooked outside, butted inside. If the hook is true they agree.

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “Why would anybody build a tool with a loose end on purpose?”

AnalyzeClassroom discussion · d=0.82
35–80

Dimensioning conventions off the reference page. Gap at the extension line. Dimensions outside the object. Number above the line. Each dimension once. Re-dimension the block sketch properly.

Extension: find a dimension on your sketch that could be derived instead of given, and remove it.

ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
80–110Trade again. Same sketch, second pass. Did the question count go down?EvaluatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Question count from 1.1 versus today is the measurable improvement. Post both numbers.

Can they explain WHY the two door readings should agree, not just report that they do?

MATERIALS & PREP

A block or plate of known length for the tape check.

One deliberately bent hook if you can sacrifice a cheap tape.

TEACHER NOTESHighest-value ten minutes in the unit. They all own the tool and almost none of them know.

title: 1.4 · Check it before you trust it
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.4 · Check it before you trust it

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can check an instrument before I use it.20 + 20 + 15☐ Calipers ☐ Known block ☐ Tapes
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20Zero the caliper closed. Does it read zero? Check the tape against a known length. Inspect the hook, jaws, blade.ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
20–40Find a tool in this room that is out. Say by how much and what it costs over a day.AnalyzeFormative assessment · d=0.68
40–55An instrument you did not check is an opinion. This goes on the front of every measuring session for the rest of the year.UnderstandClear targets · d=0.68
FORMATIVE CHECKSBy HOW MUCH is the target, not whether.
MATERIALS & PREPMis-zero one caliper before class.
TEACHER NOTESEstablish the routine now — it opens every measuring session all year.

title: 1.5 · How much you trust your own numbers
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.5 · How much you trust your own numbers

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can state my own uncertainty as a number and choose the instrument a claimed tolerance forces on me.MEASURE 45 · DRAW 35 · CLOSE 30☐ Tapes ☐ Rules ☐ Calipers ☐ Feeler gauges ☐ Packets
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–25Estimation call first: write your guess before you measure. Then five trials on the same block face, every reading recorded. High minus low is your uncertainty.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
25–45

One object, four instruments. Record the smallest mark on each. One person five times versus five people once — which spread is bigger, and what does each one tell you?

Talk moves — Apply to another's reasoning: “She says it's the tool. He says it's us. How do we settle it?”

EvaluateClassroom discussion · d=0.82
45–80

Draw the block again and write the tolerance you are claiming beside each dimension. Then say which instrument that tolerance forces you to use.

This is the join between the two strands: a drawing makes a promise and the instrument has to keep it.

AnalyzeConcept mapping · d=0.64
80–110Uncertainty sentence — “I trust my tape to about ______, because ______.” The blank is a number. Marzano self-rating on the Cycle 1 targets.EvaluateMetacognitive self-assessment · d=0.60
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Five identical readings means one reading written down five times.

Cycle 1 mastery records: read-rule, check-instrument, choose-instrument, repeatability, sketch.

MATERIALS & PREP

Same block face as 1.1 if you can get back to the fieldhouse; a spare block on a bench otherwise.

Calipers are the bottleneck — run the four-instrument work as stations.

TEACHER NOTESDo not rush the last forty minutes to get the self-rating done. The tolerance-forces-the-instrument move is the unit in one sentence.

CYCLE 2 — The name is not the size

title: 2.1 · The block, the joint, and why it comes out even
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.1 · The block, the joint, and why it comes out even

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can explain how the mortar joint makes the nominal block size work out exactly, and draw a block with its joint.MEASURE 40 · DRAW 40 · HAND IT OVER 30☐ Fieldhouse ☐ Tapes ☐ Rules ☐ Paper ☐ 2×4 offcut
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15Two weeks ago you measured a block called 16 and got 15 5/8. It is still on the board. Today we find out why.RememberSpaced retrieval · d=0.65
15–50

At the wall: measure a block — 15 5/8 by 7 5/8. Now measure a mortar joint — 3/8. Add them. Exactly 16 and exactly 8, every time. The name is not the block. It is the block plus its share of the joint. The name describes the module that repeats.

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “Why would anybody name a thing after a size it isn't?”

AnalyzeVocabulary/inductive · d=0.67
50–85Draw a block in elevation with its joint, dimensioned. Both the actual and the nominal. Add a note naming the nominal size — that note is how a real drawing carries this.ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
85–110The same trick in lumber: measure a 2×4. Trade drawings and ask one question — could the reader order material from this?EvaluatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

This is the payoff of 1.1 and the single best target in the unit. Everyone should leave able to say why the block is called 16.

The nominal note on the drawing is the check — it is the difference between a sketch and a document you can order from.

MATERIALS & PREP

Confirm you can get a tape on a joint — a raked or tooled joint reads differently than a flush one; pick a clean stretch of wall.

2×4 and 2×6 offcuts from carpentry.

TEACHER NOTES

The block is a better nominal case than the 2×4 because the reason is exact and they can prove it. Lead with the block; lumber is the second example.

Plant the module: 16 inches is the same 16 as framing on center. It gets harvested in 3.2.

title: 2.2 · Boiler room — conduit and pipe you can reach
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.2 · Boiler room — conduit and pipe you can reach

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can explain why a trade size names neither the inside nor the outside of a pipe or conduit.20 + 20 + 15☐ Boiler room access ☐ Calipers ☐ Tapes
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20Down to the boiler room. Everything the fieldhouse hangs out of reach is at arm's length here. Measure the outside of a half-inch EMT — 0.706. Measure a half-inch copper — 5/8 outside.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
20–40Neither number is a half. Copper inherited its name from old iron pipe. EMT's trade size is roughly the biggest bundle of wire you should pull through it — a name about the contents, not the container.UnderstandVocabulary/inductive · d=0.67
40–55If you are boring a hole for it, which number do you use?AnalyzeClassroom discussion · d=0.82
FORMATIVE CHECKSThe hole question is the check — first time nominal-versus-actual has a consequence.
MATERIALS & PREP

Clear the boiler room visit with facilities. Twenty students need a route and a standing spot.

If the visit falls through, bring offcuts from the shops and run it in the room.

TEACHER NOTESFour naming systems now on the table — block, lumber, copper, EMT — and four different reasons. That is the point, not the numbers.

title: 2.3 · What the gauge number counts
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.3 · What the gauge number counts

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can explain why a bigger gauge number means a thinner wire and use the three-steps-double-the-area rule.MEASURE 45 · COMPUTE 40 · CLOSE 25☐ Wire 14/12/10 ☐ Calipers ☐ Packets
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15Measure a 12-gauge wire. It is not 12 of anything. Let them hunt for what the number could be counting.AnalyzeFormative assessment · d=0.68
15–45It counts the pulls through a drawing die. More pulls, thinner wire — which is why the number runs backwards. Then measure 14, 12 and 10 with the caliper.UnderstandVocabulary/inductive · d=0.67
45–85

Area from diameter, one worked example slowly. Compute all three, divide each by the smallest. Does three gauge steps double it?

ELL/SWD: fully annotated worked example in the packet. Calculators allowed today — the comparison is the physics, not the squaring.

ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
85–110Their ratios will not be exactly 2. Is that the rule, or their calipers? That is Cycle 1 applied to Cycle 2.EvaluateClassroom discussion · d=0.82
FORMATIVE CHECKSThe scatter question is the real target — it forces them to use the uncertainty number they produced in 1.5.
MATERIALS & PREP

Stripped wire at three gauges from the electrical shop.

Most caliper-hungry session in the unit. Borrow if you can.

TEACHER NOTESDoubling the copper roughly halves the resistance. That is why wire gets fatter as the run gets longer — plant it, harvest it in Unit 6.

title: 2.4 · Four names, four reasons
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.4 · Four names, four reasons

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can use nominal, actual, tolerance and deviation correctly.20 + 20 + 15☐ All samples ☐ Packets
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20Finish the table: block, lumber, copper, EMT, wire. What it is called, what it measures, and WHY the name is what it is. Four different reasons.ApplyConcept mapping · d=0.64
20–40

Vocabulary: nominal, actual, tolerance, deviation — each in a sentence about a row of their own table.

ELL/SWD: word bank, frames and cognates in the packet.

UnderstandVocabulary/inductive · d=0.67
40–55Marzano self-rating on the Cycle 2 targets.EvaluateMetacognitive self-assessment · d=0.60
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Tolerance is what you are allowed. Deviation is what you got. They confuse these constantly.

Cycle 2 mastery records: nominal-vs-actual, joint-module, vocab, does-it-fit, dimension-and-scale.

MATERIALS & PREPAll samples on one table so the consolidation is physical, not from memory.
TEACHER NOTESThe block's reason (the joint) is exact. Lumber's is historical. Copper's is inherited. EMT's is about contents. Make them say which is which.

title: 2.5 · Does it fit, and at what scale
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.5 · Does it fit, and at what scale

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can work out whether something fits using real dimensions, and draw the result to a stated scale.MEASURE 30 · DRAW 50 · HAND IT OVER 30☐ Block ☐ EMT and copper offcuts ☐ 2" DWV ☐ Rules
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–30Measure the core of a block. Now: what would actually fit down it — a 2" drain? A run of EMT? Use real dimensions, not names. Then the classic: a nominal 2" drain in a nominal 2×4 wall.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
30–80

Scale. Half size, quarter size, and what the scale note on a drawing means. Draw the block in section with the service in it, to a stated scale, dimensioned.

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “It fits. So why do wet walls get framed in 2×6?”

ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
80–110Trade. Put a rule on the other person's drawing and check whether it is really at the scale it claims.EvaluatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Checking a drawing's scale with a rule is the assessable moment — real tradesmen do it and almost nobody teaches it.

This is the Cycle 2 Reasoning target.

MATERIALS & PREP

A cut or broken block so the cores are visible, if you can get one from the masonry side or a supplier.

Do NOT get into boring or notching limits — that is Unit 3 and it needs load first. Park it out loud.

TEACHER NOTESYour carpenters will not have known the wall decision is theirs. Your plumbers will have opinions. Let that happen.

CYCLE 3 — The survey

title: 3.1 · The layout race, and the mason's error
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.1 · The layout race, and the mason's error

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can explain why error piles up on a chain and not from a datum, and find that error in real masonry.LAY OUT 45 · MEASURE THE WALL 35 · DRAW 30☐ Fieldhouse floor ☐ Tapes ☐ Masking tape ☐ Pencils
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–30

Twelve feet on the fieldhouse floor, sixteen on center. Assign the method — half the crews measure each mark from the last one, half from one fixed end. Check where the last mark landed against 176 inches.

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “Your individual marks were fine. So where did the quarter inch come from?”

AnalyzeClassroom discussion · d=0.82
30–65Now the same thing in the wall. Count ten courses. Predict the height — ten times eight is eighty. Go measure it. If it is off, divide the miss by ten: that is the mason's average joint error, and it accumulated exactly the way your chain did.EvaluateConcept mapping · d=0.64
65–110Draw the layout as a dimensioned plan. Chain or datum — your drawing will show which one you used, and the next person has to get it right from it.CreatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

The ten-course measurement is the best assessment in the unit: a real number, off a real wall, produced by the same mechanism they just created on the floor.

Cycle 3 Reasoning target — score it on whether they can explain the drift, not on whether they drifted.

MATERIALS & PREP

Twelve continuous feet. A fieldhouse has this in abundance — it is the reason to be there.

Pick a wall stretch where ten courses are unobstructed and reachable from the floor.

Masking tape takes pencil and comes up clean.

TEACHER NOTES

Do not let crews choose their method. If they pick, the confident ones all pick datum and the comparison dies.

If the wall comes out dead on eighty inches, that is a result too — say what it tells you about the mason.

title: 3.2 · Why sixteen — and why it is the same sixteen
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.2 · Why sixteen — and why it is the same sixteen

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can explain why framing is sixteen on center and why the block module is the same module.20 + 20 + 15☐ Packets
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20Why sixteen and not fifteen? Forty-eight and ninety-six divide by it, so sheet goods land on framing. Why to centers? So the sheet edge gets half a stud and the next sheet gets the other half.UnderstandWorked examples · d=0.57
20–40Now the connection: a block is nominally sixteen long. A stud bay is sixteen on center. They are the same grid, and that is not a coincidence — the whole building is on a four-inch module.AnalyzeConcept mapping · d=0.64
40–55What would break if block were fifteen and framing were sixteen?EvaluateClassroom discussion · d=0.82
FORMATIVE CHECKS“Because that's how it's done” is a 1. “Because 48 divides by 16” is a 3. “Because the block and the stud are on the same grid” is a 3 with room to spare.
MATERIALS & PREPNothing beyond the packet.
TEACHER NOTESEvery carpenter in the room has laid out 16 on center and none of them has been told why. This is the whole course in one session.

title: 3.3 · Measuring what you cannot reach
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.3 · Measuring what you cannot reach

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can dimension something out of reach by counting a known module, and produce three views of something I can reach.COUNT 40 · DRAW 45 · HAND IT OVER 25☐ Fieldhouse ☐ Tapes ☐ Rules ☐ Paper ☐ Objects with a step
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–40

The joist bearing is thirty feet up and your tape is twenty-five. Count courses to it. Thirteen courses is a hundred and four inches, and you never left the floor. Then find two more things up there you can dimension the same way.

Extension: how would you get the height of something that isn't on a module? What else up there has a size you already know?

ApplyConcept mapping · d=0.64
40–85

Three orthographic views of something you CAN reach — a bollard, a base plate, a floor box, a bracket. Top above front, side beside it, and they line up. Straightedges from here on.

ELL/SWD: give the reference page and an object identical to the worked example.

ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
85–110Your drawing goes on the table with the objects. Somebody else picks yours out of the pile using the drawing alone.EvaluatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Counting the module to a height is the target, and it is checkable — two students should get the same answer.

Picking the object out of a pile from the drawing alone is the cleanest assessment in the unit. It either works or it does not.

MATERIALS & PREP

Count the courses to the joist bearing yourself first, and know the answer.

A pile of similar-but-not-identical objects for the three-view work — that similarity is what makes the identification real.

This is ETF task 1.3. Chapter 4, Technical Drafting, is the reading if you want it.

TEACHER NOTESSession 1.1 was freehand on purpose. This is drafting, and the switch should be announced.

title: 3.4 · Tolerance
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.4 · Tolerance

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can decide in or out, and say by how much.15 + 25 + 15☐ Packets ☐ Cardboard ☐ Scissors ☐ No calculators
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15Plus or minus what, and who decides. A mason's joint tolerance is not a machinist's. The tolerance follows the consequence of being wrong.UnderstandVocabulary/inductive · d=0.67
15–40Cut a go/no-go gauge out of cardboard for a stated dimension and tolerance. Then test the class's pieces with it. It fits or it doesn't — no argument, no judgment call.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
40–55The sort in the packet. Five specs, five measurements. In or out, and by how much. Fractions, no calculator.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
FORMATIVE CHECKS

The “by how much” column is the target. In-or-out alone is a coin flip.

The gauge makes tolerance binary and physical — watch who cuts theirs to the nominal instead of to the limits. That is the misconception.

MATERIALS & PREP

Cardboard and scissors. Cut one gauge yourself first so you know the trap.

No calculators. Subtracting sixteenths is the point.

TEACHER NOTESA go/no-go gauge has two ends for a reason: one that must fit and one that must not. Students who cut a single slot have not understood tolerance yet.

title: 3.5 · Mastery task — as-built of the wall
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.5 · Mastery task — as-built of the wall

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can verify what is there against a drawing and produce an as-built of what is actually there.WALK 20 · MEASURE 40 · WRITE 25 · DRAW 25☐ Fieldhouse ☐ Your drawing, with errors ☐ Instruments ☐ Task sheet
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20

THE WALK. No drawing yet. They go to the bay and fill in the scope sheet — what the job is, what is actually there, what has to be true to call it done, what they are stuck with, what code says, what they are not doing, what they still need to know.

This is the one place in the course where they decide what the job is instead of receiving it. Do not hand out anything until the sheets are in.

AnalyzeClear targets · d=0.68
20–30NOW hand out your drawing. Read the four scoring dimensions aloud. They already know them.UnderstandClear targets · d=0.68
30–70Instrument check first — the routine from 1.4. Then survey the bay: coursing, wall height by count, conduit runs and their supports, pipe and its fall, boxes located. Eight items with spec, tolerance and deviation.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
70–90Write the inspection. What is out, what matters most, and how much you trust your own numbers — with a number.CreateFeedback · d=0.70
90–110Produce the as-built: what is actually there, dimensioned, scale noted, nominal materials named in a note. Self-score before handing it in.CreateMetacognitive self-assessment · d=0.60
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Score all four dimensions. Grade is the lowest, never the average.

The as-built carries Communication. The uncertainty statement carries Reasoning. Catching your planted errors carries Transfer.

MATERIALS & PREP

THE ONE THING TO DO IN ADVANCE: draw one bay of the fieldhouse wall yourself, with two or three deliberate errors in it — a wrong course count, a conduit support at the wrong spacing, an overall that does not match its chain. Keep a record of the truth so you are scoring against fact, not consensus.

You are drawing the errors, not building them. A drawing is an afternoon; an assembly is a week.

Rubric posted where they can see it while writing.

TEACHER NOTES

Nothing new is introduced today. Everything on this task was taught in the last three cycles, on this wall.

Put their 1.1 freehand sketch and this as-built side by side in the portfolio. Same building, twelve sessions apart. You will not have to tell them they improved.
